Q: Is there any formal way to distinguish which store operation the current load synchronizes with? A:

Is there any formal way to distinguish which operation the load synchronizes with for this simple example?

No.

If not, does that mean we should avoid this pattern when designing wait-free/lock-free algorithms

Correct; have different writes store unique values if it matters which thread you're syncing with. A sequence number or thread-id is one possibility. Or often an array index or a pointer, so the reading thread can find the other data the writing thread "published" with its release-store.

On some real hardware (e.g. x86 and I think AArch64 and other "other-multi-copy-atomic" ISAs), an acquire-load actually synchronizes with all previous release-stores to the same location. But the C++ memory model isn't that strong because some real-world hardware also isn't; you only get that with RMWs instead of pure stores, e.g. value.store(1, release). And yes, really release is sufficient, you don't need acq_rel because of the release-sequence guarantee. (Memory ordering with multiple releases and a single acquire / What does "release sequence" mean?)

But pure stores are a lot more efficient than RMWs on most hardware (in terms of being better able to find memory-level parallelism with surrounding ops), especially when contention is low. So generally better to design algorithms to not need that.

Q: ORA-12560: TNS:protocol adapter error A:

It seems you have some sort of resource leak. Do you close connections properly ?

Also, as ar said in comment, why don't you just keep this connection open ? IIRC Establishing conn is costly operation in any DBMS.

Also, from documentation:

ORA-12560 -- TNS:protocol adapter error
Cause: A generic protocol adapter error occurred.
Action: Check addresses used for proper protocol specification. Before reporting this error, look at the error stack and check for lower level transport errors. For further details, turn on tracing and reexecute the operation. Turn off tracing when the operation is complete.

UPDATE:
Problem could be caused by overflow of Windows event journal. Check Oracle's events here:
Start menu => Control Panel => Administrative Tools => Event Viewer
You should either clear journal manually or increase its' size

Q: Is there a way to make scipy.optimize.minimize(method='trust-constr') accurate? A:

What seems to be happening is that if your initial guess has more than 8 digits correct then the evaluation of cos(x) at double precision already satisfies the minimisation constraint being equal to -1 and so scipi has nothing to do and returns the initial guess. No further improvement is possible. Some optimisers will find the ends of the range of contiguous zeros and return the mid point but evidently scipi doesn't do this.

This is more of a problem with the numerical limitations of evaluating cos(x) near an integer multiple of pi at double precision.

 cos(pi + x) ~= -1 + x^2/2 - O(x^4)

so that when |x| < 1.4e-8 (empirically 1.0395e-8) the answer will be -1.0

If you want the optimiser to be able to solve it then add one to it and use the identity:

 1 + cos(pi + x)  = 2*sin(x/2)^2

These are the plots of both functions - note how heavily quantised cos(pi+x) is! And also that evaluated by math.cos it is zero for a wide range of inputs either side of pi.

Your Newton Raphson method is actually solving the very much easier problem -sin(x) = 0 which is perfectly well behaved.

my_answer = simple_newton_solver_for_comparison(
    f=lambda x:analytic_jac([x])[0],
    df=lambda x:analytic_hess([x])[0][0],
    initial_guess=initial_guess,
  )

Should be instead

my_answer = simple_newton_solver_for_comparison(
    f=lambda x:fun([x])[0],
    df=lambda x:analytic_jac([x])[0],
    initial_guess=initial_guess,
  )

That change should make it do exactly the same as scipi when optimising fun().

If you suspect that an optimiser has not done its job correctly then stepping away from the alleged solution by a factor of (1 + sqrt(machine_eps) will give it a sporting chance of hitting the true minimum.
